name: Hunter
description:
You were here an hour before anyone else. The snare is already set in the narrow pass, the oil worked into the arrowheads before dawn. You know which direction the wind is blowing and what that means for a shot from the ridge. When the enemy arrives, the ground has already been prepared. The fight, in all the ways that matter, is already over.

Hunters don't wait for the fight to come to them. Long before arrows are nocked or traps are sprung, the Hunter has already been working—reading the terrain, following signs, preparing the ground. Their greatest advantages are usually invisible by the time combat begins: the poison applied that morning, the snare laid in position an hour before the party arrived, the knowledge of which shot from which angle will guarantee a wound too serious to walk off. When a Hunter's preparations come together, a fight can be over before most participants realize it has started.

At the center of a Hunter's combat practice is the bow—or the crossbow, or the sling, or whatever ranged weapon they have mastered. Their training makes every shot hit harder than it should, upgrading the fundamental damage of the weapon through technique rather than through a heavier draw. Careful judgment of distance lets them sacrifice range for a shot that is nearly impossible to miss, or push past normal range without the penalty that would cripple a less practiced archer. And as their skill deepens, they can fire twice in the space of a single action, the rhythm of draw, aim, release becoming as automatic as breath.

Away from combat, the Hunter is the person who keeps a party alive in the wild. Each day they choose how to apply their expertise: tracking, scouting, moving in silence through dense cover, foraging to extend the party's provisions, or simply knowing, at all times, exactly which direction is north. In the hands of someone who truly knows the land, a single blast of the hunting horn can sharpen every ally's next effort, blunt every enemy's, or clear the threat of opportunity attacks across distances that would leave most fighters helpless.

Play a Hunter if you want to:

  • Fight from range with precision and patience, making each shot count through technique, preparation, and positioning rather than volume of fire.

  • Shape the battlefield before the first blow, using traps, poison, and terrain knowledge to set conditions that favor your party before anyone else has drawn a weapon.

  • Keep the party alive in the wild, serving as guide, scout, tracker, and forager in natural environments where your expertise is the difference between a successful journey and a disastrous one.

Questions to consider when making a Hunter:

  • What do they hunt? The answer shapes everything—a hunter of animals thinks differently than a hunter of people, and a hunter of monsters differently still. Do they have a quarry they consider their true calling, or do they take whatever the work demands?

  • How did they come to their expertise? Long solitary years in the field, an apprenticeship to a master, a community tradition, or hard lessons born of necessity?

  • What is their relationship to the places they travel through? Do they feel responsible for the land, merely comfortable in it, or simply capable?

  • How do they feel about the time their methods require? Preparation, patience, and positioning favor those who are willing to wait. Is that waiting something they find natural, or do they have to work at it?

  • Have they ever lost a quarry they were certain they had? What happened, and what did they learn from it?
